To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
foundations play multiple intermediary roles, which can be grouped into four themes, and that foundations are not alone in playing these intermediary roles.

foundations are often intermediaries, and play multiple intermediary roles; the term ‘intermediary’ is used in different ways; foundations are intermediaries because of their position, resources, relationships and expertise; foundations’ intermediary roles are often overlooked; and the intermediary roles played are not always recognized or understood.

foundations can play a variety of intermediary roles that can be grouped into four themes: bringing parties to the table, capacity development and relationships, temporal bridging and sector-level or institution-level intermediation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the ways in which foundations can play intermediary roles in the development of philanthropy in the Asia Pacific region.
the role of philanthropic foundations as intermediaries in the context of their funding of civil society organisations (CSOs) in South Africa.
how foundations’ intermediary roles can be conceptualised and understood.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
foundations are intermediaries in many different ways, and in many different contexts.
foundations are ‘intermediaries’, in the sense of ‘intermediary’ as used in economics, but they are also much more.
foundations play multiple and complex intermediary roles, which are both similar to and distinct from other intermediary actors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
foundations are playing a growing role as intermediaries in a number of different ways and at different scales.
philanthropic foundations are playing a critical role in the middle of a growing philanthropy ecosystem.

philanthropic foundations play intermediary roles that can be described as: bringing parties together; capacity development and relationship-building; bridging time; and sector-level or institution building.
The main takeaway from our work is that

foundations can play a range of intermediary roles, which can be conceptualized as a spectrum, and that these intermediary activities may be complementary to, or in some cases in conflict with, other roles played by foundations.
foundations play a wide range of intermediary roles and that the term ‘intermediary’ is a poor description of the full range of roles played by foundations.
foundations can play many different intermediary roles, and the choice of which to play depends on their strategic goals and on the context in which they are operating.
